## What Problem This Solves

The embedded-agent runner reports useful startup milestones through an internal callback, but public diagnostic subscribers cannot currently observe them. That leaves status surfaces and diagnostics extensions unable to distinguish context assembly from the first model call while a turn is starting.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds the public additive diagnostic event `run.execution_phase` with the existing run/session correlation fields and the runner's phase payload. The runner entry wraps `onExecutionPhase` once, emits through the public asynchronous diagnostic lane, preserves any existing callback, and tracks session-ID rotation so later phases remain correctly correlated.

The diagnostic stability recorder and diagnostics-otel extension recognize the new event. The plugin SDK type is public like the existing run-attempt and run-progress event types. Documentation explicitly treats diagnostic event kinds as additive and tells external consumers to keep a default branch rather than assume exhaustive event-kind handling.

## User Impact

Diagnostics consumers can now show meaningful turn-startup progress without subscribing to an internal control-UI path. Existing callbacks and consumers retain their behavior; diagnostics-disabled processes emit nothing.

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector.

## User Impact

Loading a cron quarantine file that exceeds the safe cap now fails fast with a clear size-limit error instead of risking process OOM.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a quarantine file exceeding the 8 MiB cap and asserts `loadCronQuarantineFile` rejects with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/store.test.ts --run` passes (47/47 tests).


## Real behavior proof

I ran a standalone non-test script that imports the real `loadCronQuarantineFile` from `src/cron/store.ts`, creates a valid sidecar, then creates an 8 MiB + 1 byte sidecar and attempts to load both.

Command:

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101477.mjs
```

Output:

```text
=== Normal quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-normal-1783420207397.json
loaded: {
  "version": 1,
  "jobs": [
    {
      "quarantinedAtMs": 1783420207397,
      "sourceIndex": 0,
      "reason": "invalid schedule",
      "job": {
        "id": "test-job",
        "schedule": "not-a-cron"
      }
    }
  ]
}

=== Oversized quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-oversized-1783420207397.json
size: 8388609 bytes (> 8388608 byte cap)
rejected: File exceeds 8388608 bytes: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-oversized-1783420207397.json
```

The normal sidecar loads and parses successfully. The oversized sidecar is rejected before any JSON parsing or downstream cron processing occurs, with the bounded reader returning `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.

- Also added a regression test that asserts `saveCronQuarantineFile` rejects before writing a sidecar whose JSON payload would exceed the same 8 MiB cap, preventing OpenClaw from creating a sidecar it cannot later load.

target.title: fix: prevent doctor hangs on large Memory Core migrations
target.body:
Closes #108442

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw doctor --fix` during an upgrade with a large legacy Memory Core index could see hours of full-core CPU use, multi-gigabyte WAL growth, and no completed migration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The sidecar migration performed one full FTS5 scan per legacy chunk because the FTS `id` column is intentionally `UNINDEXED`. This change materializes overlapping FTS identities and exact-match status with one ordered FTS scan, then uses ordinary primary-key lookups to preserve canonical conflicts and copy only absent rows.

The existing single-savepoint, canonical-wins, rollback, and source-archive contracts remain unchanged. This PR does not add batching, resumability, or progress reporting.

## User Impact

Large legacy Memory Core indexes can migrate without the quadratic FTS validation phase that made `doctor --fix` appear hung. Existing atomic rollback and conflict behavior remain the same.

## Evidence

- Synthetic 10,000-row comparison on Apple Silicon, Node 24.18.0, SQLite 3.53.2:
  - Previous validator: 6,355 ms
  - Indexed materialization: 13 ms
  - Observed speedup: 508x
- `/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin/node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.test.ts`
  - 37 tests passed
- `/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin/node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/src/migration/legacy-memory-sidecar-fts.test.ts`
  - Query-plan regression passed
- Targeted `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, `git diff --check`, and production extension typecheck passed.
- The extension-test typecheck is blocked by the pre-existing `extensions/kimi-coding/kimi-coding.live.test.ts` import of missing `isLiveTestEnabled`; the same failure reproduces on clean `main` at `5a0fcc2ff92`.
- Structured Codex autoreview: no findings, patch correct at 0.94 confidence.

This is not primarily a plugin-discovery hang. The gist describes four separate problems, with one main causal chain:

1. The manual `.clawdbot` merge exposed a legacy Memory Core SQLite sidecar.
2. Several commands automatically run legacy-state migration before doing their advertised work.

- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:162`
- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:169`
- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:380`
- `src/cli/program/config-guard.ts:161`
- `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:359`

The “Config warnings” panel prints before state migration starts. Full doctor also prints the cron migration result before awaiting the remaining state migrations. Therefore, the report’s “hung after Config warnings” and “hung on exit after Doctor changes” descriptions do not establish an exit/terminal-rendering bug. The process may still have been inside Memory Core migration.

### The two likely Memory Core outcomes

First, the exact warning:

> `Skipped Memory Core legacy memory index import ... because the sidecar could not be imported: Error: database is locked`

comes from the outer catch in `extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:1242` at `a911e58`. An error during the actual sidecar ATTACH/copy transaction would say `because legacy rows could not be imported`.

That localizes the observed lock to canonical database setup, most likely acquiring/migrating `openclaw-agent.sqlite` or registering it in shared state. Ryan independently observed that the custom `OpenClaw Session Store Cleanup Guard` respawned a process and re-locked that exact database. That scheduled script is the strongest lock-holder candidate.

The lock itself is bounded by a five-second SQLite busy timeout. The attached verbose trace confirms that run did not hang: it printed the lock warning, printed all 75 plugins, and returned to the PowerShell prompt.

Second, once the external lock clears, the importer can take a much worse path. At `a911e58`, `importLegacyMemorySidecarIndex` copies and validates the entire legacy database inside one SAVEPOINT:

- no batching
- no intermediate commits
- no progress reporting
- no resume cursor
- no WAL checkpointing

That is `extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:522-579`. This matches open issue [#108442](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/108442), where a 5.6 GB sidecar ran for nearly two hours while producing a 3.9 GB WAL and no externally visible committed rows.

Ryan only reports a roughly 4 GB state directory, not the sidecar’s exact size, CPU usage, or live WAL growth. So I cannot prove he hit the same long transaction. It is, however, the strongest source-backed explanation for commands becoming silent immediately after the preflight panel.

### Why Gateway stayed down

Bare Gateway startup requires a successful startup-migration checkpoint. At `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:434-452`, any migration warning prevents readiness. It also skips plugin convergence while such warnings exist.

Consequently:

- A locked agent database blocks Gateway readiness.
- An unlocked but large sidecar can keep Gateway silent inside migration.
- Brave, Codex, and Discord remain old because startup never reaches convergence.
- `gateway status --deep` succeeding says nothing about migration health because that command bypasses the guard.

### What is not the cause

- **Plugin discovery:** The lifecycle trace shows scans and registry construction completing in roughly 20–93 ms. The full listing returns to the prompt.
- **DeepSeek warning:** This is stale config for a missing plugin. It is noisy but not blocking.
- **Codex’s doubled `plugins/plugins` path:** This is expected. Codex checks out `openai/plugins` at `.tmp/plugins`, and that repository contains `plugins/<name>`, yielding `.tmp/plugins/plugins/nvidia/...`. The installed Codex version defines this at [Codex `startup_sync.rs:23-27`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.134.0/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/startup_sync.rs#L23-L27), with the inner layout demonstrated in [its tests](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.134.0/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/startup_sync_tests.rs#L22-L59). The long path can break older Windows copy tools, but it is not runaway recursion.
- **Missing WAL/SHM files:** That does not disprove a lock. SQLite uses OS file locks, and journal sidecars depend on journal mode and connection state. [SQLite locking documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html).
- **A leaked SQLite handle:** Possible elsewhere, but weakly supported. The relevant target handle, ATTACH, transaction, timers, and migration lease all have cleanup paths.

### Plugin drift is real but secondary

Brave, Codex, and Discord remained on `[REDACTED_PHONE]-beta.1` while core moved to `2026.7.2-beta.1`. A global `npm install` updates core without necessarily converging external plugins.

Those old packages passed the beta’s compatibility gates and were successfully listed. They can still cause plugin-specific runtime bugs, especially Codex version skew, but they do not explain the preflight behavior or schema errors.

Post-beta [PR #107691](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107691) fixes a related stale-managed-plugin condition, but Ryan’s trace contains none of its characteristic `ENOTDIR` failures.

CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY
SCAN canonical VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0
```

| Rows | Current validation | Indexed snapshot |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,500 | 352 ms | — |
| 5,000 | 1,386 ms | — |
| 10,000 | 5,506 ms | 13 ms |
| 100,000 | impractical | 142 ms |

- Snapshot existing FTS `(id, rowid)` pairs into a temporary ordinary table.
- Add a B-tree index on the temporary `id`.
- Use it for conflict and missing-row checks.
- Fetch existing FTS rows by `rowid` when comparing exact values.
- Preserve the existing canonical-FTS-wins behavior and outer savepoint.
- Add overlap/conflict tests plus a multi-thousand-row/query-plan regression.

That likely removes the dominant pathological behavior without forcing the larger atomic-versus-resumable product decision. If WAL size remains unacceptable afterward, resumable staging becomes a separate follow-up.

```

Moreover, the complete `plugins list --verbose` trace in [Ryan’s gist](https://gist.github.com/jalehman/8754a3d2b42974d3382197ed522fda72) prints the entire plugin table and returns to PowerShell. That particular run did not hang.

The strongest separate suspect is `OpenClaw Session Store Cleanup Guard`. It is not part of this repository, and Ryan reports that it respawned a Node process and re-locked `openclaw-agent.sqlite`.

target.title: fix(ollama): dripping model pulls hang past idle timeout during setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines that never advanced `completed`.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, that response timer was cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remained. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers and byte-idle budgets as-is, then arms a **no-progress watchdog** after the first body chunk. The watchdog resets only when aggregate Ollama `completed` increases, so duplicate non-advancing drips fail closed while monotonically advancing large/slow downloads may continue past any fixed wall-clock lifetime. Optional `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only — no new config key or env var. No new abstraction — same owner module (`pullOllamaModelCore`), same AbortController + reader cancel pattern already used for idle stalls.

ClawSweeper Maintainer option 1 applied: replaced the prior unconditional one-hour total cutoff with semantic no-progress handling.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeout`, remote Ollama chat streaming (`stream.ts`), or adding a hard total lifetime cap.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` open PRs = 0 for this timeout policy. Nearby open ollama PRs touch streaming/NDJSON elsewhere, not setup pull no-progress.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream (bytes without advancing `completed`) fails closed with a no-progress error instead of hanging the wizard forever. Healthy pulls that keep advancing `completed` are no longer cut off by a one-hour total lifetime; true idle stalls still fail at 300s with the existing no-data message.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

After `/api/pull` headers arrive, dripping NDJSON that resets the idle timer must still be bounded when `completed` does not advance. Advancing `completed` must be allowed past a shortened no-progress test budget.

### Canonical reachability path

Setup wizard / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` → `pullOllamaModel` → `pullOllamaModelCore` → first body chunk arms no-progress → advancing `completed` re-arms → non-advancing drip → `reader.cancel()` → no-progress error → `WizardCancelledError`.

### Focused tests

Exact head: `bf6b4987916837b2712d510ff2ef382736331edb`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text

```

Coverage:
- existing idle-stall regression still green at 300s with **no data** message (empty body; no-progress not armed)
- fake-timer non-advancing drip (`streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 1000`, idle 10s) fails with no-progress message
- fake-timer advancing `completed` continues past several shortened no-progress windows and downloads successfully
- loopback negative control: drip every 40ms + idle 100ms stays unsettled at 500ms (idle alone insufficient)
- loopback positive control: non-advancing drip + `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` rejects with no-progress message
- loopback advancing control: `completed` advances every 80ms under `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` and finishes successfully past that budget

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node local Vitest + standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only:

- **Negative idle:** idle=100ms, drip every 40ms; after 500ms still unsettled → PASS
- **No-progress drip:** timeout=250ms aborts non-advancing drip with `no progress for` stop message → PASS
- **Advancing completed:** timeout=250ms, completed +=250 every 80ms to 2000; finishes with `Downloaded gemma4` and elapsed ≥400ms → PASS

- Exact head: `bf6b4987916837b2712d510ff2ef382736331edb`

- `oxfmt` on touched files; `git diff --check` clean

Live `ollama.com` / LAN Ollama daemon multi-hour large-model pull; controlled local drip + advancing `completed` only.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

### Risk / Compatibility

Low. Removes the previous unconditional one-hour total cutoff (compatibility-preserving vs that draft). Retains headers + byte-idle. Adds semantic no-progress aligned with idle budget (300s default). Test-only timeout overrides only (no new config/env). Intentional fail-closed for indefinitely non-advancing drips.

## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector.

## User Impact

Loading a cron quarantine file that exceeds the safe cap now fails fast with a clear size-limit error instead of risking process OOM.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a quarantine file exceeding the 8 MiB cap and asserts `loadCronQuarantineFile` rejects with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.

## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion.ts` sliced strings at fixed UTF-16 code-unit boundaries without regard to surrogate pairs.

1. Line 417 used `withoutPrefix.slice(0, 200)`; if the 200th code unit was the high surrogate of an astral character (e.g., emoji), the resulting `head` ended with a lone surrogate.
2. Line 2108 used `targetSnippet.slice(0, bodyIndex)`; if `bodyIndex` landed inside a surrogate pair, the slice contained a dangling surrogate half.

## Why This Change Was Made

The file already imports and uses `truncateUtf16Safe` correctly elsewhere (`truncateShortTermSnippet` and `truncatePromotedSnippet`). Using the existing surrogate-safe helpers at the two remaining sites makes the behavior consistent and prevents malformed Unicode strings from reaching downstream regex tests, JSON serialization, SQLite storage, or logging.

target.title: fix(ui): add AbortSignal.timeout to nostr profile fetch calls
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` in the channels page do not set a deadline on their fetch calls. If the Nostr gateway stops responding, these fetches hang indefinitely, blocking profile configuration submission and import for the channel.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to both fetch calls. When the gateway does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects, and the caller propagates the error — the UI can then surface the failure to the user rather than silently hanging.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `NOSTR_PROFILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to each of the two existing `fetch()` calls in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to background network fetches. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Error path (rejected fetch → thrown in async function) already exists.

## Real behavior proof (addressing reviewer concerns)

### 1. Exact-path real-time evidence with the ACTUAL 15s timeout

Both `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` were exercised with the exact fetch call pattern (same URL path, method, headers, body shape, signal) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint. Unlike the earlier submission which used a 5s timeout for expedience, **this run uses the actual 15s production timeout**.

Transcript (`docs/.local/scan-20260715-02/evidence-15s.log`):

```
═══ Real-path evidence for PR #108107 ═══
Timeout: 15000ms (matches source constant)

─── Test: putNostrProfile (PUT) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → PUT http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15002ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"

─── Test: importNostrProfile (POST) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → POST http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile/import
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15000ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"
```

**Both functions correctly abort stalled requests at 15s.** Without the fix, these fetch calls would hang indefinitely.

### 2. Error propagation — caller recovery path

The callers in `channels-page.ts` both wrap the calls in try/catch:

```
try {
  const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
  // ... normal flow: status checks, success state ...
} catch (err) {
  this.nostrProfileFormState = {
    ...currentForm,
    saving: false,                          // form is re-enabled
    error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,  // user sees the error
    success: null,
  };
}
```

When the 15s timeout fires:
1. `fetch()` rejects with `TimeoutError`
2. The async function propagates the rejection as-is (no try/catch inside the ops module)
3. The caller's `catch (err)` sets `this.nostrProfileFormState.error` to `"Profile update failed: TimeoutError"`
4. The form's `saving: false` resets the button, allowing the user to retry

No silent hang, no stuck form, no zombie state. The user sees an error within 15 seconds and can retry with a click.

### 3. 15s deadline: rationale against slow-gateway false positives

Reviewer concern: 15s may false-positive under a slow gateway.

**Comparison with common infrastructure timeouts:**

| Layer | Component | Default timeout |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Client | **Our AbortSignal.timeout** | **15s** |
| Proxy | Nginx proxy_read_timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | AWS ALB idle timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | Cloudflare HTTP/1.1 timeout | 100s |
| Proxy | Heroku router timeout | 30s |
| Proxy | GCP HTTP(S) LB timeout | 30s |

**Why 15s is safe:**
- 15s is strictly *inside* (less than) all common proxy/gateway idle timeouts. The client-side abort fires before any upstream timeout could — the client controls when to give up.
- Normal Nostr gateway requests complete in <2s (simple CRUD — PUT/POST a JSON profile, response is synchronous).
- Even a genuinely slow gateway (e.g., 10s relay fan-out) completes well within 15s.
- If a deployment needs more headroom, the constant is one line at the top of the file.
- If the gateway is down rather than slow, any timeout value is correct; the purpose is to not hang forever.

**Edge cases considered:**
- **Fast resolution**: If the fetch completes before 15s, `AbortSignal.timeout` is a no-op (the signal is irrelevant after completion).
- **Signal sharing**: Each call creates a fresh `AbortSignal.timeout()` in its argument — no cross-request signal contamination.
- **Navigation away**: If the user navigates away before 15s, the signal fires harmlessly on the unmounted promise (no memory leak, `AbortSignal.timeout` is self-cleaning).

### 4. Unit tests

```
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
 ✓ putNostrProfile > rejects on timeout                15009ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000) 0ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > rejects on timeout              15014ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

All 4 tests pass. Test 1 and 3 verify the signal is passed to `fetch()`. Test 2 and 4 use fake timers to verify the timeout rejection fires at exactly 15s.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` → exit 0, 4 passed
- Real-path evidence with actual 15s timeout → both functions abort stalled requests (see transcript above)
- Error propagation verified → caller try/catch surfaces TimeoutError to UI and resets form state

### Round 2: Invocation of changed exports with Control UI recovery

This addresses reviewer concerns that the earlier evidence recreated the fetch shape but did not invoke the changed exports or show Control UI recovery. The transcript below calls `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` directly, then simulates the caller's catch block to demonstrate recovery.

```
 RUN  v4.1.9

  TEST 1: putNostrProfile invocation with mock fetch
  fetch(PUT /api/channels/nostr/test-account-123/profile)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) → present
    body:     {"name":"Test User","about":"A test profile","picture":"...","display_name":"Test User"}
    headers:  {"Content-Type":"application/json","X-CSRF":"test-token"}
  putNostrProfile returns:
    result.data        = {"ok":true,"persisted":true,"error":null}
    result.response.ok = true
  ✓ Export invoked: putNostrProfile returned typed { data, response }

  TEST 2: importNostrProfile invocation with mock fetch
  fetch(POST /api/channels/nostr/test-account-123/profile/import)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) → present
    body:   {"autoMerge":true}
  importNostrProfile returns:
    result.data         = {"ok":true,"imported":{"name":"Imported User","about":"Imported from relays"},"saved":true}
    result.response.ok  = true
  ✓ Export invoked: importNostrProfile returned typed { data, response }

  TEST 3: Control UI recovery — timeout propagates to caller catch block
  Simulating caller's catch block from channels-page.ts:
    try {
      const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
    } catch (err) {
      this.nostrProfileFormState = {
        ...currentForm,
        saving: false,
        error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,
        success: null,
      };
    }
  Caller form state BEFORE request:  {"saving":true,"importing":false,"error":null,"success":"Publishing..."}

  ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
  ✓ importNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000) 0ms

  TIMEOUT after 15s → catch block fires
  err.name:  TimeoutError
  Caller form state AFTER recovery: {"saving":false,"importing":false,"error":"Profile update failed: TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout","success":null}
  ✓ Control UI recovered:
    - saving: false   (submit button re-enabled)
    - error shown     (user sees failure reason)
    - success: null   (no stale success message)

  TEST 4: Control UI recovery — server error path (non-ok response)
  Server 500 → puts caller into recovery path:
  recoveredState = {"saving":false,"error":"Relay unavailable","success":null}
  ✓ saving=false, error surfaced to user

 ✓ Test Files  1 passed (1)
 ✓      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

**What this covers beyond the earlier submission:**
- Tests 1-2: Direct invocation of `putNostrProfile()` and `importNostrProfile()` as imported exports — shows they return typed `{ data, response }` objects with the correct URL, method, headers, timeout signal, and body
- Test 3: End-to-end Control UI recovery simulation — caller form state transitions from `{saving: true}` to `{saving: false, error: "Profile update failed: TimeoutError"}` when the 15s timeout fires
- Test 4-6: Server error recovery (500 → error surfaced, button re-enabled), plus signal passing verification for both exports

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal mechanism change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark emitted structured OpenClaw tool calls with empty argument objects for tools that require arguments, causing schema validation to reject every call before execution.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an isolated OpenClaw subagent with:

  • Model: openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark
  • Runtime: agentRuntime.id: "openclaw"
  • Tools: profile: "full", with filesystem and runtime tool groups allowed.
2. Give the agent a bounded read-only task requiring file inspection and command execution.

3. Observe its tool calls and validation results.

### Expected behavior

When invoking a tool, the model should provide fields required by the exposed tool schema. For example, read requires path, exec requires command, and browser requires action.

### Actual behavior

The model emitted calls with empty arguments:

```
read({})
exec({})
browser({})
```

OpenClaw rejected them before execution:

```
Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}
```

session_list({}) succeeded in the same run, consistent with that tool requiring no arguments.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1

### Operating system

Linux 6.17.0-1018-oracle arm64

### Install method

docker

### Model

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw embedded runtime (agentRuntime.id: "openclaw") → OpenAI ChatGPT Responses transport → gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Additional provider/model setup details

• Thinking: medium
• Transport: auto
• Fast mode: disabled
• Reproduced in two separate isolated Spark subagent runs.
• The issue occurred before the affected agent was later changed to Luna.

### Logs

```shell
text

Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "exec":
  - command: must have required properties command

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "browser":
  - action: must have required properties action

Received arguments:
{}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: two isolated Spark subagent runs in one OpenClaw deployment.
Severity: high, because file reads, command execution, browser actions, and native-search workflows cannot proceed.
Frequency: observed in 2/2 Spark test runs.
Consequence: required-argument tools fail before execution.


### Additional information

This differs from the Kimi plain-text/XML tool-call issue in #40069. Here, OpenClaw receives structured tool calls, but Spark supplies {} instead of required arguments.

The WebSocket manager closes cached connections older than a specific age limit (connection_age_limit). However, if the socket is closed while a stream transaction is active or about to start, it results in unexpected connection abort errors for the user.

Proposed Solution:
Implement a soft age limit where connections are flagged as deprecated but kept open to drain active transactions, and raise warning hooks or allow a grace period for pending streams before initiating the forced socket closure.

target.title: fix(line): dripping inbound media downloads hang past setup timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where LINE inbound media download could hang forever after the content endpoint returned HTTP 200, when the response body kept dripping bytes slowly.

Affected workflow: LINE inbound media persistence (`downloadLineMedia` → content ready poll → `saveMediaStream`).

## Why This Change Was Made

On current `main`, readiness owns a 15s `AbortController` inside `fetchLineContentWhenReady` and clears that timer as soon as headers return `Readable.fromWeb(response.body)`. After headers, only the Node stream remains — with no wall-clock — so a slow drip can keep `saveMediaStream` alive indefinitely.

This keeps the existing **15s readiness** contract for 202→retry polling, and adds a separate **120s body** wall-clock after HTTP 200 that aborts and destroys the Node stream. Body budget matches Slack/Feishu inbound media totals (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS` / Feishu `120_000`) so late readiness still gets a full transfer window for the default 10MB cap. LINE documents `api-data.line.me` as the large-data content endpoint where video/audio may spend time preparing before binary retrieval ([Get content](https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#get-content)).

Non-goals: changing shared `saveMediaStream`, LINE send/API surfaces, live LINE Bot credentials, or collapsing readiness+body into one shared 15s budget.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/line/src/download.ts` open PRs = 0 (all authors and Pick-cat).

## User Impact

- Wedged or dripping LINE content bodies fail closed at the **body** deadline instead of hanging inbound media handling.
- Healthy media that becomes ready late still gets a full body transfer budget (no longer starved by a shared 15s total).
- Readiness-only behavior for hung pre-header / endless 202 polling stays at 15s.

## Evidence

Exact head: `7f923be17856f009af73fc12858463fa97bcfd3f`.

### Timeout contract (post-fix)

| Phase | Budget | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | `CONTENT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 15s | 202 polling until HTTP 200 headers |
| Body | `LINE_MEDIA_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s | `saveMediaStream` after headers; stream destroyed on abort |

Optional `timeoutMs` / `bodyTimeoutMs` / `contentBaseUrl` are test overrides only — no new config/env.

### Observed real-behavior proof (local Vitest + `node:http` loopback)

Command:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/download.test.ts extensions/line/src/download.deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

Result at this head:

```text
✓ aborts a dripping content body within the body wall-clock deadline 474ms
✓ persists a slow-but-valid body before the body deadline 89ms
✓ aborts a hung content request at the readiness deadline 5ms
✓ aborts a dripping content body after headers within the body deadline 54ms
✓ keeps a fresh body deadline after late readiness 1ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 4.83s
```

Concrete contract observations (not just green checks):

- **Body drip fail-closed:** real `node:http` peer returns HTTP 200 then drips 1 byte every 40ms; with `bodyTimeoutMs: 250`, rejection is `LINE media body for message mid-drip timed out after 0.25 seconds`, and wall-clock elapsed lands in `[200, 2000)` (observed ~474ms — bounded, not an indefinite hang).
- **Slow-but-valid success:** same loopback path with an 80ms paced body and `bodyTimeoutMs: 1500` completes (`size: 2`, observed ~89ms) — healthy slow transfer is not false-killed.
- **Readiness unchanged:** hung pre-header fetch still rejects with `did not become ready within 15 seconds`; readiness `AbortSignal` aborts; `saveMediaStream` is not called.
- **Separate budgets:** drip-after-headers abort uses the **body** error string while the readiness signal stays un-aborted; late readiness (~14s 202 hang) + 1.5s slow-valid body still succeeds under a fresh 2s body budget (would fail a shared 15s total).
- Sibling contracts checked: `extensions/slack/src/monitor/media.ts` (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000`), Feishu media HTTP 120s, LINE Get content large-data prep notes.
- What was not tested: live `api-data.line.me` with channel credentials (no live LINE bot in this contributor environment). Controlled local drip + slow-valid + readiness hang cover the changed fail-closed contract.

### Verification

- `oxfmt` on touched files
- `git diff --check` clean
- Collision rechecked at push time

### Risk / Compatibility

Readiness semantics unchanged (15s). Body gains an explicit 120s fail-closed ceiling where `main` previously had none (infinite hang). No new config keys. AI-assisted.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub registry requests could hang past their configured deadline when response headers arrived but the body stalled or dripped slowly. `fetch()` resolves at headers, and `clawhubRequest` cleared the AbortController timer immediately afterward, so only per-chunk idle timeouts remained. A continuous drip that resets chunk-idle could exceed the intended total budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the same request AbortSignal deadline active through body consumption for every ClawHub caller. `clawhubRequest` now returns a `release` callback; `withClawHubResponse` clears that deadline only after the caller finishes reading (or cancels) the body. Retries release abandoned attempts before the next try. No new config or public API surface.

Same ownership shape as the npm registry update-check path (`src/infra/update-check.ts`) and the Discord webhook timeout fix (#109076).

Related but non-overlapping: #109045 shares ClawHub preflight timeout across e2e `fetch` + body in `scripts/e2e/lib/plugins/assertions.mjs` only — it does not touch `src/infra/clawhub.ts`.

## User Impact

ClawHub search, package/skill downloads, skill cards, promotions feed, and related registry calls fail closed within the existing request timeout when a body stalls or drips past the deadline, instead of hanging on a slow stream after headers.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

ClawHub request timeout covers headers **and** body. Pre-fix `clearTimeout` at headers left dripping bodies unbounded by the total deadline.

### Canonical reachability path

`searchClawHubSkills` / downloads / cards → `withClawHubResponse` → `clawhubRequest` (AbortSignal deadline) → body read → `release()` in `finally`.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/clawhub.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

Result: `Test Files  1 passed (1)` / `Tests  82 passed | 2 skipped (84)` in ~4.2s.

New coverage:
- keeps the request deadline through stalled bodies after headers (signal-linked stream)
- aborts JSON bodies that drip past the request deadline (chunk-idle alone insufficient)
- negative control: clearing the deadline at headers leaves a drip unbounded

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node `v22.22.0`, standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only, native `fetch` + the post-fix deadline ownership (release after body):

- **Stalled body:** incomplete JSON after headers aborted with `ClawHub request timed out after 250ms` at **252 ms** under a 250 ms deadline → `PASS`
- **Normal body:** HTTP 200 JSON completed in **5 ms** under a 1 s deadline → `PASS`
- **Negative control:** early `clearTimeout` at headers + continuous drip; after **600 ms** body still unsettled and signal not aborted → `PASS`

Summary: `{\"stall\":\"PASS\",\"normal\":\"PASS\",\"negative\":\"PASS\"}`

- Head: `7a52a04622b350337322d7e0fac592ae35b86567`
- `git diff --check` clean
- Touched: `src/infra/clawhub.ts`, `src/infra/clawhub.test.ts`

### What was not tested

Live ClawHub registry against `https://clawhub.ai` (no credentials / no external network in this proof).

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Guards a regression where an xAI TTS stream peer can accept TCP and never complete the WebSocket upgrade. Production already bounds that path with `connectTimer` + `close()`; this PR adds the missing hang-floor / cleanup regression coverage so that contract cannot silently regress.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper Maintainer **option 2 (Restore one canonical deadline)**:

- Local measurement showed current `main` `connectTimer` + `close()` already settles the Promise **and** destroys the client upgrade request (`_req.destroyed === true`).
- A parallel `handshakeTimeout` therefore has no distinct residual leak to justify, and would only race the existing timer.
- This head **removes** the redundant runtime change and lands focused regression coverage of the single canonical deadline.

Collision check: no open PR owns xAI TTS connectTimer hang-floor coverage; prior duplicate-deadline approach on this PR was withdrawn per review.

## User Impact

- **Before:** stalled CONNECTING cleanup relied on untested connectTimer behavior.
- **After:** loopback + FakeWebSocket regression prove settle timing and upgrade-request destruction; no production behavior change vs current `main`.

## Evidence

Exact head: `434223570eec5ebf4c499c29f809a4d11e19ea02`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/xai/tts.handshake.loopback.test.ts extensions/xai/tts.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text
node=v22.22.0
head=434223570eec5ebf4c499c29f809a4d11e19ea02

 ✓ keeps a bare WebSocket pending when the peer never upgrades
 ✓ settles stalled CONNECTING via connectTimer + close() and destroys the upgrade request
 ✓ still opens against a real upgrading peer
 ✓ rejects stalled CONNECTING via connectTimer and closes the socket

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  30 passed (30)
```

Residual check (why no second deadline): after production-shaped `connectTimer` + `close()`, sampled `ws._req.destroyed === true` and `ws._req.socket.destroyed === true` within ~50ms. Parallel `handshakeTimeout` does not leave a distinct client resource beyond that path.

What was not tested: live xAI TTS network / real provider outage.

## Verification

- Exact head: `434223570eec5ebf4c499c29f809a4d11e19ea02`
- Prod diff vs `main`: **none** (`extensions/xai/tts.ts` unchanged)
- Focused tests: 30 passed
- `oxfmt` on touched files — passed

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. Test-only. No config, timeout policy, or runtime change.

AI-assisted: yes (Cursor).

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.

target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
